definition: A disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
clues: This is a way energy travels
It transfers energy but not matter
Light and sound are examples
A periodic disturbance that carries energy from place to place — the medium vibrates but overall doesn't move with the wave

definition: A wave where the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. Examples: light, water waves, all EM waves.
clues: This is a type of wave
The vibrations are at right angles to the direction of travel
Light and water waves are examples
A wave where displacement is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer — all EM waves and water waves are this type

definition: A wave where the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Example: sound waves.
clues: This is a type of wave
The vibrations are parallel to the direction of travel
Sound waves are an example
A wave where displacement is parallel to the direction of energy transfer — sound waves travel as compressions and rarefactions

definition: The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its rest position. Measured in metres (m). Larger amplitude = more energy.
clues: This is a property of a wave
It is measured from the rest position to the maximum displacement
A larger value means more energy
The maximum displacement from equilibrium — larger amplitude means a louder sound or a brighter light

definition: The distance between two successive identical points on a wave, e.g. crest to crest or compression to compression. Symbol: λ, measured in metres (m).
clues: This is a property of a wave
It is the distance from one point to the next identical point
Its symbol is the Greek letter lambda (λ)
The distance between two successive crests (or compressions) — measured in metres; longer wavelength = lower frequency

definition: The number of complete waves passing a point per second. Symbol: f, measured in hertz (Hz).
clues: This is a property of a wave
It is measured in hertz
It is the number of complete waves per second
The number of complete oscillations per second — measured in Hz; related to wavelength by the wave equation v = fλ

definition: The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point. T = 1/f. Measured in seconds (s).
clues: This is a property of a wave
It is measured in seconds
It is the reciprocal of frequency
The time for one complete oscillation — T = 1/f; if frequency is 50 Hz, the period is 0.02 s

definition: The speed at which a wave travels through a medium. Calculated using: v = fλ (wave speed = frequency × wavelength). Measured in m/s.
clues: This is a property of a wave
It is calculated from frequency and wavelength
Its equation is v = fλ
The speed at which the wave pattern moves — v = fλ; for EM waves in a vacuum this is always 3 × 10⁸ m/s

definition: The highest point of a transverse wave, where displacement is at its maximum positive value.
clues: This is a feature of a transverse wave
It is the highest point of the wave
It is the point of maximum positive displacement
The peak of a transverse wave — the point where displacement is at its maximum upward value

definition: The lowest point of a transverse wave, where displacement is at its maximum negative value.
clues: This is a feature of a transverse wave
It is the lowest point of the wave
It is the point of maximum negative displacement
The valley of a transverse wave — the point where displacement is at its maximum downward value

definition: A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are pushed closer together, creating a high-pressure region.
clues: This is a feature of a longitudinal wave
Particles are pushed closer together in this region
It is a high-pressure region
A high-pressure region in a longitudinal wave where particles are bunched together — the equivalent of a crest in a transverse wave

definition: A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are spread further apart, creating a low-pressure region.
clues: This is a feature of a longitudinal wave
Particles are spread further apart in this region
It is a low-pressure region
A low-pressure region in a longitudinal wave where particles are spread apart — the equivalent of a trough in a transverse wave

definition: The bouncing of a wave off a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The wave changes direction but not speed or frequency.
clues: This is a wave behaviour
A wave bounces off a surface
The angle in equals the angle out
When a wave hits a surface and bounces back — angle of incidence = angle of reflection; the wave does not change speed or frequency

definition: The angle between the incoming wave (or ray) and the normal to the surface at the point of incidence.
clues: This is an angle measured in ray diagrams
It is measured between the incoming ray and the normal
It is always measured from the normal, not the surface
The angle between the incident ray and the normal at the surface — always measured from the normal, not from the surface itself

definition: The angle between the reflected wave (or ray) and the normal to the surface. Always equals the angle of incidence.
clues: This is an angle measured in ray diagrams
It is measured between the reflected ray and the normal
It is always equal to another angle in the same diagram
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal — always equals the angle of incidence (the law of reflection)

definition: An imaginary line drawn perpendicular to a surface at the point where a wave meets it. Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal.
clues: This is an imaginary line used in ray diagrams
It is perpendicular to the surface
All angles of incidence and reflection are measured from it
A line at 90° to the surface at the point of incidence — all ray angles are measured from this line, not from the surface

definition: The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in wave speed.
clues: This is a wave behaviour
A wave changes direction as it crosses a boundary
It is caused by a change in wave speed
Bending of a wave as it crosses from one medium to another — caused by a change in speed; a faster medium bends away from the normal

definition: The angle between the refracted ray and the normal at the point where the wave enters the new medium.
clues: This is an angle measured in refraction diagrams
It is on the transmitted side of the boundary
It is measured from the normal
The angle between the refracted (transmitted) ray and the normal — smaller than the angle of incidence when entering a denser medium

definition: A property of a medium that determines how fast light travels through it. A denser medium slows light down more and causes greater refraction.
clues: This is a property of transparent materials
It determines how much light slows down in the material
A higher value means light travels more slowly
A measure of how much a medium slows light — higher optical density = slower light = greater bending at the boundary

definition: When a wave travelling in a denser medium hits the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle and is completely reflected back into the medium.
clues: This is a phenomenon in optics
It occurs when light hits a boundary at too steep an angle
The light is completely reflected back into the denser medium
When the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, all light is reflected back — the basis of optical fibres and diamond brilliance

definition: The angle of incidence above which total internal reflection occurs. At this angle, the refracted ray travels along the boundary.
clues: This is a threshold angle in optics
Beyond this angle, total internal reflection occurs
At exactly this angle, the refracted ray travels along the boundary
The angle of incidence at which the refracted ray lies along the boundary — above this angle, total internal reflection occurs

definition: A longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects that travels as compressions and rarefactions through a medium. Cannot travel through a vacuum.
clues: This is a type of longitudinal wave
It requires a medium to travel through
It cannot travel through a vacuum
A longitudinal wave of alternating compressions and rarefactions — travels through solids, liquids and gases but not through a vacuum

definition: How high or low a sound seems — determined by its frequency. Higher frequency = higher pitch.
clues: This is a property of sound
It is determined by frequency
Higher frequency gives a higher value
The perceived highness or lowness of a sound — determined by frequency; a violin has higher pitch than a bass guitar

definition: How loud or quiet a sound seems — determined by its amplitude. Larger amplitude = louder sound.
clues: This is a property of sound
It is determined by amplitude
Larger amplitude gives a louder sound
The perceived volume of a sound — determined by the amplitude of the wave; shouting has larger amplitude than whispering

definition: Sound waves with a frequency above the upper limit of human hearing (above 20,000 Hz). Used in medical imaging and sonar.
clues: This is a type of sound wave
Its frequency is above the range of human hearing
It is used in medical scanning and sonar
Sound with frequency above 20,000 Hz — beyond human hearing; used in baby scans, sonar and cleaning delicate instruments

definition: A reflected sound wave. Used to measure distances — the time taken for an echo to return can be used to calculate the distance to a surface.
clues: This is a phenomenon involving sound waves
It is caused by reflection of sound
It can be used to measure distances
A reflected sound wave — the time delay between the original sound and the echo allows distance calculation using speed of sound

definition: A device used to display waveforms of sound waves, showing amplitude, frequency and wave shape on a screen.
clues: This is a piece of laboratory equipment
It displays wave patterns on a screen
It shows amplitude and frequency of sound waves
An electronic device displaying voltage vs time — used to show the waveform of a sound; amplitude and frequency can be read from the trace

definition: The family of transverse waves that all travel at the speed of light (3 × 10⁸ m/s) in a vacuum. Arranged in order of frequency/wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma.
clues: This is a family of waves in physics
All members travel at the same speed in a vacuum
They are ordered by frequency and wavelength
A continuous range of transverse EM waves from radio (low frequency) to gamma (high frequency) — all travel at 3×10⁸ m/s in a vacuum

definition: The longest wavelength, lowest frequency part of the EM spectrum. Used for TV and radio broadcasting and satellite communication.
clues: This is a type of EM wave
It has the longest wavelength in the EM spectrum
It is used in broadcasting and communication
The lowest frequency EM waves — used for radio and TV broadcasting, satellite communication and MRI scanners

definition: EM waves used in cooking (absorbed by water molecules) and in mobile phone and satellite communication.
clues: This is a type of EM wave
It is used in cooking and mobile communication
It is absorbed by water molecules
EM waves between radio and infrared — absorbed by water molecules in food (cooking) and used in mobile phone and satellite communication

definition: EM waves emitted by all objects as heat. Used in thermal imaging cameras, remote controls, and optical fibre communication.
clues: This is a type of EM wave
It is emitted by all warm objects
It is detected as heat
EM radiation between microwaves and visible light — all objects emit it; used in thermal cameras, remote controls and optical fibres

definition: The narrow band of the EM spectrum that the human eye can detect. Ranges from red (longest wavelength) to violet (shortest wavelength).
clues: This is the part of the EM spectrum we can see
It spans from red to violet
Red has the longest wavelength in this range
The small portion of the EM spectrum detected by the human eye — red has the longest wavelength, violet the shortest

definition: EM waves with shorter wavelengths than visible light. Causes tanning and skin damage. Used in sterilisation and detecting forged banknotes.
clues: This is a type of EM wave
It has shorter wavelength than visible light
It causes tanning and can damage skin
EM waves just beyond violet light — causes tanning and skin cancer; used in sterilisation and security marking detection

definition: High-frequency EM waves that pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone and dense materials. Used in medical imaging.
clues: This is a type of EM wave used in medicine
It passes through soft tissue but is absorbed by bone
It is used for medical imaging
High-frequency EM radiation that penetrates soft tissue but not bone — used in medical X-ray imaging and airport security scanners

definition: The shortest wavelength, highest frequency part of the EM spectrum. Emitted by radioactive nuclei. Used in cancer treatment and sterilising medical equipment.
clues: This is a type of EM wave
It has the highest frequency in the EM spectrum
It is emitted by radioactive nuclei
The most energetic EM waves — emitted from radioactive nuclei; used in cancer radiotherapy, sterilisation and PET scanners

definition: The speed at which all EM waves travel in a vacuum: 3 × 10⁸ m/s (300,000,000 m/s).
clues: This is a fundamental constant in physics
All EM waves travel at this speed in a vacuum
It is approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s
3 × 10⁸ m/s — the speed of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum; the fastest anything can travel

definition: Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, creating ions. UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionising. Can damage cells and DNA.
clues: This is a type of radiation
It can remove electrons from atoms
UV, X-rays and gamma rays are examples
High-energy radiation that ionises atoms by removing electrons — can damage living cells and DNA; UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionising

definition: Radiation emitted by a perfect absorber and emitter of all wavelengths. The hotter the object, the more radiation emitted and the shorter the peak wavelength.
clues: This is radiation emitted by a perfect absorber
Hotter objects emit more of it at shorter wavelengths
The Sun approximates this type of emitter
Radiation from a perfect emitter — hotter objects emit more radiation and at shorter peak wavelengths; explains why stars have different colours

definition: As the temperature of an object increases, the intensity of radiation emitted increases and the peak wavelength decreases (shifts towards shorter wavelengths).
clues: This describes a relationship in physics
As an object gets hotter, its peak radiation wavelength decreases
Hotter objects emit more radiation overall
Higher temperature → more radiation emitted + peak wavelength shifts shorter — explains why very hot objects glow blue-white, cooler ones glow red
